Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Russia Russia ‘losing 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit’ Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day but western officials say it cannot keep up with casualty level Peter Walker Senior political correspondent Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.05 EDT Last modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia is losing about 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit, western officials have said. While Russia is still acquiring new battlefield recruits at speed, with an estimated rate of 1,000 a day, in the last two months even this has not been sufficient to replace those killed or injured. “We estimate that the gap between the number of people Russia is losing to casualties and the number they’re being able to recruit is around 6,000 a month at the moment,” one western official said. “Putin’s response to this has been to escalate himself and to target civilian infrastructure and civilians in Ukraine, firing over 360 missiles since early July and exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of defence against ballistic missiles. It’s clear that Moscow intends to try and break Ukrainian morale by destroying its energy infrastructure this winter.” Such tactics are in part because Putin has limited options for overcoming the huge losses on the battlefield with more recruitment. Western officials believe further mobilisation would be a big risk both politically and economically, saying the last such event, in autumn 2022 , saw about a million – often highly skilled – Russians leave the country, with less than half returning. It is also unclear whether the Russian military could absorb the several hundred thousand new recruits which would result, given a lack of equipment and officers. Ukraine has repeatedly attacked Russian targets connected to oil, creating fuel shortages, but has appealed repeatedly for more help from allies, both with offensive missiles and defence systems. View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK will share information about Storm Shadow missile components with Kyiv. Photograph: Ukrainian presidency/Sipa/Shutterstock Andy Burnham visited Kyiv on his first overseas trip as prime minister this week. He told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK would give Ukraine previously classified information on the British-manufactured components for long-range cruise missiles. Burnham has also urged the international community to do more to protect Ukraine against Russian attacks, particularly with more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles. He is expected to make this argument at next month’s UN general assembly in New York. In response, Russia has made repeated threats of retaliation, including talk of attacks on UK military targets both inside and outside Ukraine. The western officials said that while the threat from Russia remained very real, the situation had not changed, and the assessment was that “Putin absolutely wants to avoid a direct confrontation with Nato”. One official said: “We are seeing a continuation of hostile rhetoric and various accusations against the UK. This is absolutely consistent with longstanding Russian military doctrine, which is to use rhetoric to both exploit fears in adversaries and to influence decision-making. So this is not a new phenomenon.” Ukraine war briefing: Missiles shot down during long Russian attack wave Read more Officials say Russia still has the capability to target the UK, with cyberattacks or physical attacks on civilian targets by proxies, for example on factories or warehouses. Last year, six men were jailed for their involvement in an attack ordered by Russia against a warehouse in east London housing aid to Ukraine. But officials said their assessment was that Putin would limit any such action to avoid more direct conflict with Nato. Putin’s overall aim in Ukraine, western officials believe, is to maintain a campaign of attrition, hoping that support from Ukraine’s allies will ebb away, particularly if governments are spooked by public alarm over Russian threats. Such threats should be seen, one official said, as attempts to create a “fractured and more vulnerable Europe”. Another said: “It’s important to keep in mind that this is not new. Russia has invoked the threat of the possible use of nuclear weapons numerous times in recent years to try to scare us into ending support for Ukraine.” Explore more on these topics Russia Ukraine Foreign policy Europe Vladimir Putin Nato news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Russia says UK ‘playing with fire’ amid reports CIA chief has warned Kremlin not to attack Nato Yorkshireman believed to be first Briton to die fighting for Russia against Ukraine UK officials prepare for potential Trump talks as Burnham plans New York trip Burnham’s visit to Kyiv marks a renewal of badly needed support for Ukraine Burnham says UK with Ukraine ‘all the way’ despite ‘outrageous threats’ from Russia – Europe live Burnham accuses Russia of ‘outrageous threats’ against UK as he visits Kyiv On Donetsk’s ‘life or death’ highway with the Khyzhak brigade – photo essay The Audio Long Read ‘The war leaked into every lesson’: learning Ukrainian in a country under siege – podcast Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.liverpoolecho.co.uk/news/liv.text: A Huyton teenager who feared she would have to face GCSE resits has celebrated getting the grades she needed to pursue her lifelong love of horses. Weronika Wojtas, 16, was “ecstatic” after opening her results at Lord Derby Academy this morning (Thursday, August 20) and discovering she had done better than she expected. The teenager achieved grades of four 5s, two 4s, two 6s, and one 8 in Polish and is now heading to Myerscough College to study Level 3 Equine Management. Weronika told the ECHO : “I think I’ve done really well. Honestly, I was expecting 3s and 4s and thought I would have to resit in college and take the lower course, but then I saw the exact results I needed. “I couldn’t have asked for anything better.” The first person Weronika ran to after opening her results was her mum, who she said had motivated her throughout the stressful revision period. She said: “She was the person who motivated me to keep going and told me it would all be worth it in the end. She’s just as happy as me - she’s ecstatic. “Now, seeing my results, the only person I have to thank is my mum. She’s the person who motivated me the most to get the grades that I did.” Weronika's love of horses began when she was just five years old, after her dad would take her to visit and feed horses in a field near the East Lancs. She said: “Ever since then, I was always like, ‘Oh my God, I love horses, I love horses’. I started horse riding when I was five, and I rode for around nine or 10 years. I stopped last year, sadly, because of GCSEs and all kinds of different stuff, but it taught me loads and further helped my love for horses.” Now preparing for the next chapter, Weronika hopes to get back into riding through Amazonka UK, a Polish showjumping group, while studying at Myerscough. Her course will cover areas including horse biology and behaviour, with the opportunity to take part in riding. Weronika said: “I don’t see a career without horses. It’s a big part of my personality, so I’d say it’s quite known.” She added that she was also grateful to have the opportunity to pursue a future in the sport. She said: “Especially with it being such an expensive sport, I feel really grateful for the opportunities I’ve been given.” Weronika, whose family are Polish, was also particularly pleased with her grade 8 in Polish after taking the subject as an external GCSE. She said: “My entire family are Polish. They all live in Poland, but my parents moved here not long after they got married and then had me. “Before school, I was only taught Polish, so my first language was Polish. Then, at primary school, that’s where I started to pick up English. “I found out I could do Polish as an external exam for my GCSEs, which I’m glad I took on as I got an 8 out of it.” There was little time for relaxing after results day, with Weronika heading straight to Myerscough for her enrolment appointment after discovering she had secured her place on the course. But afterwards, she planned to celebrate with her family - and perhaps take advantage of one of the rumoured GCSE results-day freebies. She said: “I’m hoping to celebrate with Nando’s and my family, if the rumours are true, you get it free. “Most importantly, after I leave now, I’m going straight to Myerscough for my enrolment appointment because I got onto my course. “Then I can celebrate for the rest of the day.”

Ginger Livingston/ The Daily Reflector Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Dozens of people lobbied the Greenville City Council to halt plans to use Flock cameras in the city, saying the device marketed as an investigative tool is eroding privacy rights. About 20 speakers and their supporters gathered outside Greenville City Hall conference room 337 on Monday to lobby against using the cameras, also known as automated license plate readers, in the city. The council did not meet in its chambers because it planned to immediately go into a closed session discussion after opening the meeting. Instead, the council extended its typical 30-minute public comment session to an hour to hear everyone who signed up. The intent of Flock cameras is to locate missing people, stolen vehicles and gather evidence to locate criminal suspects, but you have to consider other uses, said Kyla McClain, co-chairman of the Young Democratic Socialists of America, East Carolina University chapter. “When you give the government access to information (about) where ordinary people drive, we have to ask who is watching the people watching us,” McClain said. Richard Braman, a public health student at East Carolina University, said his family immigrated to the United States in 1985 from Czechoslovakia, a police state with mass surveillance and people spying on their neighbors. “Mass surveillance contractors are a gateway to a mass surveillance state and a threat to the freedoms and liberties that form the foundation of the United States,” Braman said. “The city allowing the Flock system to be set up is the beginnings of a very eerily similar system that was present in Czechoslovakia.” There have been 27 incidents of wrongful detention according to the Institute of Justice, a nonprofit law firm, Braman said. The Washington Post reported at least 50 law enforcement officers nationwide have been charged with or accused of misusing the system, he said. A Mooresville police officer was arrested, accused of using Flock 31 times to track her boyfriend’s ex-wife, one person said. Other speakers shared similar stories from across the nation. The city should direct the money budgeted for Flock cameras towards training officers in mental health crisis counseling, Braman said. The Greenville Police Department already has surveillance cameras in operation, said former councilwoman Marion Blackburn. That system is different because it’s monitored by Greenville police, not artificial intelligence, she said. Flock is a private company, Blackburn said, it gathers the information and distributes it to local law enforcement. However, the data is on a marketplace, available to anyone. A Texas police offer used Flock more than 2,300 times to stalk an ex-girlfriend, Blackburn said. An officer in another community used Flock 717 times to track his estranged wife, Blackburn said. A 23-year-old woman was jailed for two weeks when Flock incorrectly identified her car as being at an accident scene. “I would like my daughter to grow up in a place where she doesn’t have to be watched all the time,” said William Brady. “I don’t think she needs to be watched when she’s going down a slide by somebody in a data center somewhere.” When he moved to Greenville in 2013 he wouldn’t have taken his daughter to the Town Common or downtown because those areas weren’t great. “Things have changed,” Brady said. The change came from the community working to improve public spaces, not through surveillance, he said. “I can’t think of a single time where constant surveillance has helped anybody,” Brody said. Citizens must stand up and fight for their personal liberties, said Andrew Moghaddam. “How much surveillance are we willing to accept in our daily lives?” he said. Marketed as a crime-fighting tool, Moghaddam said, “What they actually create is a vast surveillance network to track the movement of ordinary citizens who have done absolutely nothing wrong. “The assumption seems to be that everyone should be monitored just in case they might, someday, become a suspect,” he said. “That turns a fundamental principle of a free society on its head. In America we are supposed to be innocent until proven guilty, not tracked until proven innocent.” The Greenville Police Department announced in early July that 10 Flock cameras would be deployed at strategic locations throughout the city. The department said the cameras are used to help investigators locate missing and endangered people, investigate crimes and enhance public safety. The department’s announcement said in 2024, Flock cameras helped investigators identify a vehicle connected to a homicide and locate a missing person. Acting Police Chief KZ Thomas said the 10 cameras have not been installed. City Manager Michael Cowin said staff needed further discussions with council about when or if the cameras are installed. The Pitt County Board of Education in April unanimously voted to let the Pitt County Sheriff’s Office place Flock cameras in front of Wellcome Middle and Chicod schools. A sheriff’s office spokesman said the agency has more than two dozen Flock cameras set up throughout the county. Mayor P.J. Connelly thanked participants as the speakers left the council meeting. “We appreciate the conversation and discussion. Speaking for myself, I thought it was very reasonable and helpful. A lot of the comments made today made me think about this, moved the needle a bit,” Connelly said. Dedan Waciuri of the Amani Collective, a social justice group, addressed the Flock protesters outside the council conference room. He said the cameras are another tool in the over policing segments of the Greenville community experience. “We would like to bring this conversation to the community, make it broader, to create a collision of community members,” Waciuri said. “I love the conversation of surveillance, repression and control in certain parts of the community.” Ginger Livingston can be contacted at glivingston@apgenc.com and 252-329-9570.
